stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Corran Spring?
stimulus: Hydrologists studying the Arlen Plateau have mapped forty-two springs, and nearly all of them flow at a steady rate through every season. These springs draw on a deep limestone aquifer that can hold water for decades. The exception is Corran Spring. It is fed instead by a thin layer of sand resting on clay, and that layer fills only during spring rains. As a result, Corran Spring dries up by late summer each year and does not flow again until the following spring.
choices: It flows steadily in every season because it draws on a deep aquifer.
It stops flowing for part of each year because its water source is shallow.
It draws on the same limestone aquifer as the plateau's other springs.
It has been studied more closely than any other spring on the plateau.
explanation: The text says Corran Spring is fed by a thin sand layer that fills only during spring rains, and that it dries up by late summer. Put those two sentences together and you get a spring that stops flowing for part of the year because its source is shallow and seasonal.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Steady flow from a deep aquifer is true of the other springs. The text names Corran Spring as the exception to it.

C.why: You put the spring in the wrong category. The text says it is fed 'instead' by a sand layer, not by the limestone aquifer the other springs share.

D.why: This sounds scientific, but nothing in the text says how much the spring has been studied. You can't point to a line that supports it.

stem: What does the text indicate about the Carrow Bay version of "The Salt Bride"?
stimulus: Folklorists have recorded more than three hundred versions of a tale known as "The Salt Bride" along the northern coast. In nearly all of them, a woman who came out of the sea goes back into it at the end of the story and leaves her husband on shore. A version recorded in the fishing village of Carrow Bay reverses this ending. In it, the bride stays on land, and it is the husband who walks into the sea.
choices: It ends with the bride returning to the sea, as most versions do.
It was recorded earlier than any other version found on the coast.
It leaves out the husband and tells the story only from the bride's side.
It changes which character goes into the sea at the end of the tale.
explanation: The text says the Carrow Bay version 'reverses this ending': the bride stays and the husband walks into the sea. So the version changes which character leaves for the sea.

A.why: You described the typical version instead of the exception. The bride returning to the sea is how 'nearly all' versions end, and the text says Carrow Bay reverses that.

B.why: The text never says when any version was recorded. Calling it the earliest goes beyond what the passage supports.

C.why: The husband is central to the Carrow Bay ending, because he is the one who walks into the sea. The version does not leave him out.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the dark-coated bumblebee species?
stimulus: In a survey of a high mountain meadow, ecologists found that most bumblebee species there stop foraging once the air temperature falls below 10°C, which usually happens in the early morning and evening. One dark-coated species, however, was recorded gathering nectar at temperatures as low as 4°C. The researchers suggest that its dark coat absorbs sunlight and helps keep its flight muscles warm.
choices: It stops foraging once the air temperature drops below 10°C.
It forages mainly at night, when the other species are inactive.
It stays active at temperatures colder than the other species tolerate.
It has a lighter coat than the other bumblebee species in the meadow.
explanation: After 'however', the text says this species was recorded foraging at 4°C, while most species stop below 10°C. Putting the two facts together, it stays active in colder conditions than the others do.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Stopping below 10°C is what 'most bumblebee species' do. The 'however' sentence marks this species as different.

B.why: You confused the kind of difference. The species differs in what temperatures it can forage at, not in the time of day it forages. The text never mentions night foraging.

D.why: The text calls this species 'dark-coated' and credits the dark coat for its tolerance of cold. A lighter coat reverses that.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Line 7?
stimulus: In a two-year field trial, agronomists grew twelve wheat varieties on plots that received half the usual amount of irrigation. Eleven of the varieties produced about a third less grain than they did with normal watering. Line 7, however, produced nearly the same amount of grain under both conditions. When the researchers dug up the plants, they found that Line 7's roots reached almost twice as deep as those of the other varieties.
choices: Its grain output held steady with less water, and its roots grew deeper.
Its grain output fell by about a third, as did that of the other varieties.
Its roots were shallower than those of the other varieties in the trial.
It has since been adopted by farmers in regions that often face drought.
explanation: The text says Line 7 produced nearly the same amount of grain with reduced irrigation, and that its roots reached almost twice as deep as the others'. This choice combines both facts.

B.why: You described the group instead of the exception. The one-third drop applies to the other eleven varieties. 'However' marks Line 7 as the variety that did not follow that pattern.

C.why: The text says Line 7's roots went almost twice as deep as the others'. This choice reverses that.

D.why: The passage reports only a field trial. Nothing in it says farmers have adopted the variety.

stem: What does the text indicate about tissue-resident memory T cells?
stimulus: Memory T cells are immune cells that recognize pathogens the body has encountered before, and most of them travel continuously through the blood and lymph nodes. However, one group, known as tissue-resident memory T cells, stays in a single location, such as the skin or the lining of the lungs. Because these cells are already stationed where many infections begin, they can respond to a returning pathogen before circulating cells arrive.
choices: They travel continuously through the blood and the lymph nodes.
They stay in one tissue, so they can respond early where infections begin.
They respond to a returning pathogen only after circulating cells arrive.
They are the most abundant type of memory T cell found in the body.
explanation: The text says these cells stay in a single location and, because they are stationed where infections begin, they can respond before circulating cells arrive. This choice combines where they stay with what that lets them do.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Continuous travel through blood and lymph nodes is true of most memory T cells, and 'However' introduces the group that stays put.

C.why: The text says these cells respond 'before circulating cells arrive.' This choice reverses the order.

D.why: This sounds scientific, but the text never compares how many there are of each type. Nothing in the passage supports calling them the most abundant.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the dune sedge?
stimulus: In a survey of fourteen sedge species in a coastal salt marsh, ecologists found that nearly all of them grew only where tides flooded the soil every day. The dune sedge was the exception: it grew mainly on higher ground that is flooded only during storms. The researchers suggest that its unusually deep roots may let it reach fresh groundwater there.
choices: It grew only in soil that the tides flooded every day, like most of the surveyed species.
It grew mainly in places that the tides reach less often than the other species' locations.
It has deeper roots than any other plant that ecologists have studied in salt marshes.
It was the only sedge species that the ecologists were unable to find in the marsh.
explanation: Collect the sentences about the dune sedge. The other species grew where tides flooded the soil daily, and the dune sedge grew mainly on higher ground that floods only in storms. Put together, that means it grows where tides reach less often. That is a restatement in different words, which is what this subtype rewards.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Daily flooding is true of nearly all the other species, and the passage says the dune sedge is the exception.

C.why: The passage calls its roots 'unusually deep', and it only uses that as a possible explanation. It never compares them with every salt-marsh plant ever studied. This sounds scientific, but you can't point to a line that supports it.

D.why: The ecologists did find the dune sedge, on the higher ground. You may have mixed up 'exception' with 'missing'.

stem: What does the text indicate about the six warehouses that also cut scheduled hours?
stimulus: Economist Rana Idowu studied forty warehouses that raised their starting wages in 2023. At most of them, the share of workers who quit fell within a year, as expected. At the six warehouses that also cut scheduled hours, however, quit rates stayed roughly the same. Idowu suggests that for those workers, higher hourly pay may have been offset by smaller weekly paychecks.
choices: Their quit rates fell within a year, just as quit rates did at most of the other warehouses.
They kept starting wages at earlier levels rather than raising them as the others had done.
They raised starting wages but did not see the drop in quit rates that most others saw.
They lost more workers than any other warehouses that Idowu had previously studied.
explanation: All forty warehouses raised starting wages, and that includes the six. The sentence after 'however' says their quit rates stayed roughly the same, while most others saw a drop. Put those two facts together and you get C.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Falling quit rates describe most warehouses, but 'however' marks the six as different.

B.why: The study covers only warehouses that raised starting wages, so the six raised them too. What they did differently was cut hours.

D.why: The passage says only that their quit rates stayed about the same. It never compares them with Idowu's earlier studies, so this claims more than the text supports.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the gray-crowned warbler?
stimulus: Banding records from Tessaly Island show that eleven warbler species breed there each summer. Ten of them fly south in autumn to spend the winter in Central America. The gray-crowned warbler also leaves the island in autumn, but tracking tags reveal that it travels west instead, to coastal forests on the mainland only about 200 kilometers away.
choices: It stays on Tessaly Island through the winter rather than migrating like the other species.
It spends the winter in Central America along with the other warblers that breed on the island.
It migrates in a different direction from the other warbler species that breed on the island.
It is the warbler species that researchers have tracked most often on Tessaly Island.
explanation: The ten other species fly south, and the gray-crowned warbler 'travels west instead.' Both groups migrate, but they go in different directions. You can put your finger on each half of that.

A.why: You mixed up the category of difference. The passage says it 'also leaves the island in autumn,' so it does migrate. What differs is the direction, not whether it migrates at all.

B.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Central America is where the other ten species winter. The gray-crowned warbler goes to the mainland to the west.

D.why: The passage mentions tracking tags but never says this species was tracked more than the others. It sounds plausible, but no line supports it.

stem: What does the text indicate about the cables on the Marrow River Bridge?
stimulus: When steel bridge cables corrode, engineers often replace the entire cable system. On the Marrow River Bridge, however, inspectors found that only the cables near the eastern anchorage had corroded, because rainwater from an adjacent road pooled there. Rather than rebuild the whole system, the city replaced those cables alone and redirected the road's drainage.
choices: Corrosion was limited to cables in one area of the bridge, where water had collected.
Corrosion had spread through all of the cables, so every one of them was replaced.
Corrosion struck the eastern cables because they were made of a weaker type of steel.
Corrosion was caused mainly by salt spray blowing up from the river below the bridge.
explanation: Two sentences give the answer: only the cables near the eastern anchorage had corroded, and they corroded because rainwater pooled there. Combine those and you get corrosion confined to one area where water collected.

B.why: You described the general practice from the first sentence instead of this bridge. After 'however', the passage says only some cables corroded and only those were replaced.

C.why: The passage gives a cause, pooled rainwater, and says nothing about the type of steel. This invents an explanation that no line supports.

D.why: The passage says the water came from the road, not the river. You attached the right topic, corrosion, to the wrong source.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the pyramid-shaped loom weights?
stimulus: At a Bronze Age settlement, excavators recovered dozens of clay loom weights, most of them shaped like rings. A few, however, were pyramid-shaped, a form otherwise known in the region only from sites at least 300 kilometers to the south. Archaeologist Mirela Dunca suggests that weavers moving north may have brought them, though she notes that they could also have been traded.
choices: They were the most common kind of loom weight that the excavators found at the settlement.
They prove that weavers from southern sites moved north and settled at this location.
They were made from a different kind of clay than the ring-shaped weights at the site.
They match a form previously found in the region only at sites located far to the south.
explanation: The passage says the pyramid shape is 'otherwise known in the region only from sites at least 300 kilometers to the south.' D says the same thing in different words.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Most of the weights were ring-shaped, and only 'a few' were pyramid-shaped.

B.why: Dunca only suggests that weavers 'may have' brought them, and she offers trade as another possibility. 'Prove' ignores those hedge words.

C.why: The passage separates the weights by shape, not by material. Nothing in it mentions differences in clay.
